The HOST project was initiated in October 1980 and completed in late 1987.
For commercial aircraft engines in the foreseeable future, compressor discharge temperature will exceed 922 K (1200 °F), while turbine inlet temperature will be approximately 1755 K (2700 °F).
Military aircraft engines will significantly exceed these temperature values.
Hot section maintenance costs account for almost 60 percent of the total engine maintenance costs.

The HOST project developed improved analytical models and computer codes for predicting the aerothermal environment, thermomechanical loads, material behavior, structural response, and life prediction of critical hot section components.
The project involved research across six technical disciplines: instrumentation, combustion, turbine heat transfer, structural analysis, fatigue and fracture, and surface protection.

Researchers generally followed a common approach of investigating relevant phenomena through benchmark experiments, evaluating and improving analytical models, and validating the models against the experimental data.
One advanced structural design concept investigated was the segmented combustor liner, which divided the standard full-hoop liner into segments to eliminate life-limiting high hoop stresses.

To improve predictive capability, researchers focused on better understanding the basic physics, emphasizing local and global conditions, accommodating nonlinear and inelastic behavior, and expanding models from two to three dimensions.
The HOST project involved over 70 separate research and technology development activities, including work conducted through contracts, grants, and in-house efforts at the NASA Lewis Research Center.
The project results were disseminated through numerous publications, including six annual workshops with conference proceedings and a comprehensive bibliography.
Advanced high-temperature materials investigated included directionally solidified, single crystal, and oxide-dispersion-strengthened superalloys.

The improved analytical models and computer codes developed in the HOST project were expected to lead to reduced maintenance costs and increased engine performance and efficiency for advanced turbine engines.
The project aimed to better ensure improved durability of future hot section engine components during the design process.
Accurate life prediction of hot section components is challenging due to the complex cyclic high-temperature operation they experience.
